PLECAS_TITULOS_6: FOUNDATION OF THE COALITION OF FEMINIST WOMEN (CMF), THE FIRST ALLIANCE OF FEMINIST GROUPS IN MEXICO IN 1976

COMENTARIOS:
COALITION OF FEMINIST WOMEN (CMF). First alliance of feminist groups in Mexico founded in mid-1976. Sponsored by the National Women's Movement (MNM) and the Mexican Feminist Movement (MFM), of which Yan María Castro Yaoyólotl—one of the two co-founders of the first lesbian-feminist group in Mexico, the Lesbos Group founded in 1977—was a co-initiator.
Ákratas, due to its separatist position, did not join the Coalition since liberal feminism (petty-bourgeois middle class) prevailed in it and because it was totally heterocentered (centered on heterosexuality).
FUENTE:
FEM Magazine, No. 163. 
20th Anniv. Our History
ARTICULO: On modest naives and fierce fighters

PLECAS_TITULOS_6:
FOUNDATION OF ÁKRATAS 1976-1980. ÁKRATAS GROUP 1976-1980. 
RADICAL, ANARCHIST, SEPARATIST AND FEMINISM FIRST

COMENTARIOS:
FOUNDATION OF THE ÁKRATAS GROUP. Grupo Ákratas was the first Mexican feminist group explicitly composed of heterosexual and lesbian women and led particularly by the latter. It was founded by Marcela Olavarrieta, another ephemeral Mexican woman, and four foreigners—two Scandinavians and possibly one German and one American—who were part of the traveling women's movement of the late 60s and 70s, "the nomads." It is unknown if they started the group in France where Marcela was pursuing postgraduate studies or upon arriving in Mexico, but it was toward the end of 1976, possibly in November (according to research with those who knew the group). 
Ákratas was an irregular group; however, it nevertheless laid the ideological and political foundations for both the feminist lesbian movement (FL) (four decades later: lesbofeminism) and the lesbian feminist movement (LF) that would develop starting the following year, 1977.
FUENTE: Bandera Socialista Newspaper. No. 79. PRT, Trotskyist party
ARTICULO: Photograph of Marcela Olavarrieta

COMENTARIOS:
ÁKRATAS GROUP AND SEPARATISM. Ákratas only participated in some events organized by the lesbian groups Lésbos (1977) and Oikabeth I (1978), due to its radical and separatist stance, it had great ideological differences with the former, for being liberal and petty-bourgeois, middle class; and with the latter, for being socialist, depending on an ideology created by men. 
Ákratas considered that only the self-organization of women as an autonomous political force could combat patriarchy, since mixed organizations always kept women in a subordinate place and did not address their specific demands.
Ákratas at a feminist meeting organized by Lésbos and Oikabeth I in Cuernavaca, Morelos, 1978.
ARTICULO: Marcela Olavarrieta at the Second Meeting of Heterosexual Feminists and Lesbian Feminists in Cuernavaca, Morelos

TITULO_COMENTARIOS: OFF OUR BACKS MAGAZINE ARTICLE ON ÁKRATAS
COMENTARIOS:
OFF OUR BACKS MAGAZINE ARTICLE ON ÁKRATAS. 1980 article presenting the political and organizational perspective of the Ákratas group: composed of lesbian and heterosexual women; radical anarchist separatist feminist political definition; no link with the gay homosexual movement due to its misogynistic ideology; double oppression: being women and being lesbians. 
Main objectives: women's liberation and combating patriarchy. 
Internal organization: construction of a non-patriarchal organization, without hierarchy, central leadership, or concentration of power; small consciousness-raising groups with horizontal network autonomy; decisions by consensus; goals and strategies; study circles; individuality, not masses. Small consciousness-raising group: authentic bonds of solidarity, cohesion, efficacy and congruence; discovering how patriarchy prevents solidarity among women; women's organization to combat patriarchy.
FUENTE: Off Our Backs Magazine, Vol. 10. No. 1
ARTICULO:
Ákratas-Lesbian Feminism in 
Mexico

TITULO_COMENTARIOS: INTERNATIONAL TRIBUNAL ON CRIMES AGAINST WOMEN
COMENTARIOS:
INTERNATIONAL TRIBUNAL ON CRIMES AGAINST WOMEN. In March 1976, in Brussels, the International Tribunal on Crimes against Women was held, organized by feminist activists; Simone de Beauvoir said it marked the beginning of the decolonization of women.
For lesbian feminists, the issue of violence against women was fundamental (unlike for gay women), not only because lesbians were women, but because they identified politically with heterosexual women as their natural allies (and not with homosexual-gays), and because they knew that the emancipation of lesbianism depended on the emancipation of all women. The tribunal was attended by nearly 3000 women from 33 countries.
ARTICULO: Tribunal on crimes against women

TITULO_COMENTARIOS: POLITICAL PARTICIPATION OF MARCELA OLAVARRIETA IN THE 1968 STUDENT MOVEMENT
COMENTARIOS:
POLITICAL PARTICIPATION OF MARCELA OLAVARRIETA IN THE 1968 STUDENT MOVEMENT. 
Marcela Olavarrieta participated in the 1968 student insurrection in Xalapa, Veracruz, days before the massacre carried out by the Mexican army against students and civilians on October 2 in Tlatelolco. Facing military persecution, she left Jalapa hidden in a car heading to Mexico City to avoid arrest and was forced to abandon her academic and professional activities as a political fugitive.
When, after many years, lesbian feminists learned of this fact, she became a revolutionary icon.
FUENTE: El Mundo de Córdoba. Link to page
ARTICULO: History of a woman from Cordoba on October 2, 1968 in D.F. Marcela Olavarrieta Marenco.

COMENTARIOS: MARCELA OLAVARRIETA IN PARIS, FRANCE. In the mid-70s, Marcela was studying a postgraduate degree in Paris, France, where she had the great opportunity to experience the height of the feminist movement of the 60s-70s, "the second wave." As part of this great experience, she met many Latin American women combatants, political exiles from several countries, proscribed from their places of origin to separate them from their anti-imperialist and anti-capitalist political activity. One group that stood out was the Brazilian exiles who edited a newsletter-magazine called "Nosotras" from 74 to 76, which had great influence in several parts of Latin America and in Brazil itself to promote the feminist movement. Marcela was part of this magazine and is cited by the editor itself, the prominent Brazilian political exile Danda Prado.
FUENTE:
School of Communication and Arts (ECA) of the University of São Paulo (USP). 
Journalism and citizenship center.
ARTICULO: Nosotras: feminist press in exile and the discovery of gender

COMENTARIOS:
MARCELA OLAVARRIETA. Photograph of Marcela Olavarrieta, the main co-founder of Ákratas, in an article in the Bandera Socialista newspaper of the Revolutionary Workers' Party (PRT), Trotskyist, expressing with her hands one of the most representative symbols of the feminist movement.
Marcela thought that men, both from the right and the left, capitalists or socialists, had a programming of thousands of years of being dominant and conquerors, therefore, they always tried to prevent women's emancipation. 
For the same reason, it was the women themselves who had to struggle to break the chains of their own slavery, but their proximity to them did not allow them, first, to visualize themselves as oppressed and exploited and, second, to break with thousands of years of dependence and subordination regarding them. 
Therefore, an indispensable condition to overcome said dependence was separating totally from them and identifying with other women, and that was lesbian feminist love.
FUENTE: Bandera Socialista Newspaper. No. 79. PRT, Trotskyist party
ARTICULO:
Quadruple oppression of lesbians: 
OIKABETH

COMENTARIOS:
POLITICAL STANCE OF MARCELA OLAVARRIETA. Marcela was politically located within the current of international radical feminism (FR), in contrast to liberal feminism (FL) because the latter, besides being pro-capitalist, constituted a gear in the patriarchal machinery and perpetuated the slavery of women; liberal feminists did not aim to change the system, but to adapt and integrate into it (adaptationism and integrationism).
Likewise, she did not sympathize with the homosexual movement because she considered that men, both heterosexual and homosexual, were beneficiaries of the patriarchal system and both were andro-phallo-centrist and therefore, misogynistic.
FUENTE:
Photographic Studio 
Of Ana Victoria Jiménez
ARTICULO: Photographs of Marcela Olavarrieta

COMENTARIOS: UNDERGRADUATE THESIS. Marcela conducted anthropological research in indigenous communities with which she established great empathy. She was particularly interested in traditional healing practices and beliefs, reclaiming them against institutional hegemonic medicine and rescuing much of indigenous wisdom.
ARTICULO: Magic in the Tuxtlas, Veracruz

COMENTARIOS: MOTIVOS DE NARCISO. Collection of poems by Marcela Olavarrieta with an uncompromising and disturbing tone, which expects no consent, just as she was herself.
ARTICULO: Motivos de Narciso

PLECAS_TITULOS_6: IDEOLOGICAL-POLITICAL DIFFERENCES OF MARCELA OLAVARRIETA WITH NANCY CÁRDENAS

COMENTARIOS:
MARCELA OLAVARRIETA AND NANCY CÁRDENAS. Marcela and Nancy had great ideological differences. Marcela was a radical-anarchist-separatist feminist and Nancy was a homosexual-gay-integrationist; Marcela started from feminism and Nancy from gayism; Marcela from total independence from men and Nancy from dependence on homosexuals (Monsiváis and "the boys in the band"). Marcela fought for the political autonomy of women, self-organization, and Nancy was opposed to the constitution of an exclusive movement of lesbians, accusing it of being divisive and exclusionary, besides opposing the "high-sounding and aggressive word, lesbianism."
Marcela and Nancy at the First Meeting of Heterosexual Feminists and Lesbian Feminists organized by Lésbos and Oikabeth I at Nancy Cárdenas's house, Cuernavaca, Morelos. 1978.
ARTICULO: Photograph of Marcela Olavarrieta and Nancy Cárdenas. First Meeting of Heterosexual Feminists and Lesbian Feminists organized by Lesbos and Oikabeth I.

TITULO_COMENTARIOS: WHY MARCELA YES AND NANCY NO
COMENTARIOS: WHY MARCELA YES AND NANCY NO. Fragment of a lecture presented at UAM-Xochimilco in April 2001 in the Forum: Homosexual Movement in Mexico, on the history of the lesbian-feminist movement, by Yan María Castro Yaoyólotl. Where she explains why for the Mexican lesbian-feminist movement the political reference was never Nancy Cárdenas but Marcela Olavarrieta, and why, in fact, the lesbian-feminist movement broke all ties with Nancy due to said ideological-political differences in 1979 and never established contact with Nancy again. The dilemma was: Marcela, radical separatist feminism or Nancy, moderate integrationist gayism.
ARTICULO: Why Marcela yes and Nancy no. Why the historical reference of the Mexican lesbian-feminist movement is Marcela Olavarrieta and not Nancy Cárdenas

TITULO_COMENTARIOS: SABOTAGE BY THE "VOCES EN TINTA" BOOKSTORE OF THE ÁKRATAS PRESENTATION
COMENTARIOS: SABOTAGE BY THE "VOCES EN TINTA" BOOKSTORE OF THE ÁKRATAS PRESENTATION. The "Voces en tinta" bookstore, in coordination with AHMLFM-YMY, had scheduled for day x of x the PowerPoint presentation of Ákratas. But at the moment the presentation was to begin, a film titled "Ákratas" about the Spanish Civil War began (the bookstore being a place that focuses on LGBT matters). This act clearly intended to confuse the public and sabotage the presentation of the lesbian feminist Ákratas. The bookstore administrator was not there and never showed up, and the copy of the PowerPoint was lost. Lesbian groups saw it as clear LGBT sabotage, and one of the employees assured that it was not the bookstore's responsibility, that there was "external intervention" referring to Lizarra.
ARTICULO: Ákratas 1976, the beginning of the lesbian feminist movement in Mexico
FECHA: PowerPoint presentation, February 3, 2018, Voces en Tinta Bookstore

COMENTARIOS:
SEX-GENITAL MARKET OF GLOBALIZATION. 
1975 marks the beginning of the infiltration of a new, completely anti-feminist vision of women within feminism itself—an ideological virus. This offensive was not initially identified by feminists due to the postmodern handling and manipulation of rhetoric, bizarre and cryptic narrative, and language as a weapon of penetration and domination. It was not until 1978 that this anti-feminism evidenced its hidden purpose: to dismantle the fundamental bases of feminism. It was Gayle Rubin's book: The Traffic in Women: Notes on the 'Political Economy' of Sex, published in 1975, that marked the beginning of the dismantling of feminism—specifically radical feminism (FR) of the 60s-70s "second wave,"—establishing the foundations for genderist ideology (Gender Theory (TG)). This rupture would manifest in full in 1978 with the onset of the famous "feminist sex wars" that characterized the 80s in the U.S.
ARTICULO: The Traffic in Women. Notes on the political economy of sex
